pages.title: Graph and local graph
pages.description: The knowledge graph of the whole vault — 10,000 notes and 50,000 links — and the local graph of the open note, with filters, colour groups and full keyboard use.
pages.md:
## The graph

**Knowledge Graph** (command palette) shows every note of the vault, and a line
for every `[[link]]` between two notes.

- **Big vaults.** The graph is built from the vault index, so the notes
  are not read again. The layout is computed in a background worker; the
  picture appears at once and settles over a second or two. Nodes and
  links are drawn with WebGL, so 10,000 notes and 50,000 links pan and
  zoom smoothly. While you move the view, a sample of the links is drawn;
  all of them come back as soon as you stop.
- **Filters.** Narrow the graph by **tag** (nested tags included:
  `project` keeps `project/active`), by **folder** (and its subfolders),
  or by a frontmatter **property**: `status=open`, or just `status` for any
  note that has one.
- **Colour groups.** Colour the notes by their top folder or their first
  tag. The legend shows the twelve biggest groups.
- **Labels** show for the bigger notes, and for more of them as you zoom
  in. Hebrew names are shaped and written right to left.

## Structure: tree and sunburst

A ```structure block draws the vault's folders, its nested tags
(`#project/lumen/ui`) or this note's headings as a tree or a sunburst:

```structure
source: tags        # folders | tags | headings
view: sunburst      # tree | sunburst
root: project       # optional: only under this folder or tag
```

- Each item shows how many notes are under it (headings: how many headings).
- In Hebrew the tree grows from the right, and the sunburst runs
  counter-clockwise from the top.
- "Show as a tree" swaps the picture for an outline tree. **Tab** to it,
  then ↓ / ↑ move, the arrow toward the text's end opens an item or goes
  to its first child (← in Hebrew, → in English), the other arrow closes
  it or goes to its parent, Home / End go to the ends, and **Enter**
  opens the note or jumps to the heading.

## The local graph

**Show / hide the local graph** opens a panel beside the note: the open
note in the middle, and the notes within **1, 2 or 3** links of it. It has
the same tag and folder filters, and is coloured by folder. It follows you
as you open other notes, and opens in well under a fifth of a second.

## The time slider

"Up to" narrows the graph to the notes dated up to a day — by **Last saved**
or by **Created** (the note's `created` property, else its `date`). Notes
with no such date always stay. It works together with the tag, folder and
property filters, and the table view lists exactly the notes the graph
draws. In Hebrew the slider runs right to left; ←/→, Home and End move it,
and Play steps through the days. It is the same slider as the entity
graph's.

## With the keyboard

The graph is one focusable area. Tab to it, and:

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| ← ↑ → ↓ | go to the linked note in that direction (or, if there is none, the nearest note that way) |
| Enter | open the focused note |
| + / − | zoom in / out |
| 0 | fit the whole graph |
| Shift + arrows | pan |
| Home | back to the biggest note (in the local graph: the open note) |

The focused note's name and number of links are announced to screen
readers. In the full graph, the **Find a note** box jumps to any note by
name, so every note can be reached without a mouse.

pages.title: Daily notes and the Hebrew calendar
pages.description: The calendar's holidays, fasts and weekly Torah portion, for Israel or the diaspora, and the {{holiday}} and {{parasha}} placeholders of the daily note.
pages.md:
**Show / hide the calendar** (command palette) shows a month under the file tree. A day with a daily
note is marked; clicking a day opens its note, or creates it from your
template.

## Holidays and the Torah portion

The calendar knows the Jewish year: the festivals, the fasts, Rosh Chodesh,
the Israeli national days, and the Torah portion of every Shabbat.

- Days with a holiday or a fast have a mark on top. Hover a day, or reach
  it with a screen reader, for its civil date, its Hebrew date, its holidays
  and, on Shabbat, its portion.
- Under the grid, the month's holidays are listed by day.
- Names are in Hebrew when the UI is in Hebrew, and in English otherwise.

### Israel or the diaspora

The festivals have one day of yom tov in Israel and two in the diaspora, so
the two calendars differ: Simchat Torah, the eighth day of Pesach and the
second day of Shavuot are diaspora days only. When one of them falls on
Shabbat, Israel reads the next Torah portion that week, and the two
schedules realign a few weeks later, when the diaspora reads two portions
together and Israel reads them separately.

The **⚙ settings** of the calendar have a checkbox,
**Holidays and Torah portions as in Israel**. Until you change it, Lumen
picks Israel when the UI is in Hebrew or your time zone is Israel's.

### What is included

| | |
|---|---|
| Festivals | Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur, Sukkot with Chol HaMoed and Hoshana Raba, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah, Pesach with Chol HaMoed, Shavuot |
| Fasts | Tzom Gedaliah, 10 Tevet, Ta'anit Esther, Ta'anit Bechorot, 17 Tammuz, Tish'a B'Av |
| Other days | Chanukah, Tu BiShvat, Purim Katan, Purim, Shushan Purim, Pesach Sheni, Lag BaOmer, Tu B'Av, the eve of the festivals, Rosh Chodesh |
| Israeli days | Yom HaShoah, Yom HaZikaron, Yom HaAtzmaut, Yom Yerushalayim |

Fasts that fall on Shabbat move as they do in practice: Tzom Gedaliah,
17 Tammuz and Tish'a B'Av to Sunday, Ta'anit Esther and Ta'anit Bechorot to
Thursday. Yom HaShoah, Yom HaZikaron and Yom HaAtzmaut move as Israeli law
sets them, so that they never touch Shabbat.

## In the daily note

Two placeholders join `{{date}}`, `{{hebrewDate}}`, `{{weekday}}` and
`{{title}}` in the daily-note template:

| Placeholder | Becomes |
|---|---|
| `{{holiday}}` | the day's holidays, separated by `·`, or nothing |
| `{{parasha}}` | this week's Torah portion (the Shabbat on or after the day), or the festival read instead |

For example, the template

```markdown
# {{title}}

{{hebrewDate}} · {{parasha}} {{holiday}}
```

gives, on Friday 16 May 2025 in Israel, a line with the Hebrew date,
`Emor` and `Lag BaOmer` (in a Hebrew UI: `פרשת אמור` and `ל״ג בעומר`).

## The Hebrew-month view

A ```hebrew-calendar block shows the daily notes on a month of the Hebrew
calendar — Tishrei to Elul, with Adar I and Adar II in a leap year — with
each day's holidays and the Shabbat reading, and under it the year's
writing activity (notes saved per day) by Hebrew month:

```hebrew-calendar
heatmap: true      # false: the month only
```

In a `.base`, `type: hebrew-calendar` (with `date:`, default `date`) puts
each note of the view on its day.

- **Tab** to the month, then ← / → move a day (in Hebrew ← is the next
  day), ↑ / ↓ a week, Home / End the ends of the week, PageUp / PageDown
  the month before or after, and **Enter** opens the day's note (a Base:
  the first note on that day). Each day reads out its Hebrew and Gregorian
  date, holidays and portion.
- The heatmap has a row per Hebrew month and a column per day of the month
  (day 1 on the right in Hebrew), and "Show the table" gives its numbers.
- Gregorian calendar charts can't do this: their calendar is Gregorian only,
  so this view is drawn by Lumen itself from the same calendar as the daily
  note.

## How it is computed

The calendar is Lumen's own code: the fixed Hebrew calendar (the molad and
the four postponements of Rosh Hashana), the holiday rules, and the rules
for which Torah portions are read together, from the Shulchan Aruch. No
calendar library is used; the common one is under the GPL, which Lumen
does not ship. A whole year — holidays and every Shabbat, for Israel and
for the diaspora — is computed in a few milliseconds, in your browser.

The tests check the arithmetic against the browser's own Hebrew calendar on
every day from 1990 to 2060, and every holiday rule against a hand-checked
table of the years 2025–2030.


## Your morning

`⌘K` → **Daily note: “Your morning”** adds a block to today's note, and from
then on writes it each morning when you open today's note. It is off until
you run it, and `⌘K` → **Daily note: turn off “Your morning”** stops it.

The block has:

- the Hebrew date, this week's parasha and today's holidays;
- the notes changed since the last morning, newest first (daily notes are
  left out);
- the open tasks due today or earlier. Due dates can be written as
  `📅 2026-11-12` (Tasks), `[due:: 2026-11-12]` (Dataview) or
  `@due(2026-11-12)`;
- how many review cards are waiting, with the first few.

Every row links to its note or card.

Everything comes from this device: the vault index that search keeps in
memory, `.lumen/review.json` and the Hebrew calendar. Nothing is sent
anywhere. On a 10,000-note vault the block takes a few milliseconds, once
the index is built.

The block sits between `<!-- lumen:morning:start -->` and
`<!-- lumen:morning:end -->`. Writing it again replaces only that part, so
your own text in the note stays as it is. While today's note is open with
edits, the block is written into the editor instead of the file.

## Learning plans

`⌘K → Learning plans…` lists four study cycles, each with today's reading
and a link to its text on Sefaria:

| Cycle | A cycle | Started |
|---|---|---|
| Daf Yomi | 2,711 days, a folio a day | cycle 14 on 5 January 2020 |
| Mishnah Yomit | 2,096 days, two mishnayot a day | 20 May 1947 |
| Daily Rambam, one chapter | 1,017 days | 29 April 1984 |
| Daily Rambam, three chapters | 339 days | 29 April 1984 |

Both Rambam cycles start with the Mishneh Torah's introduction (the
transmission of the Oral Law, the positive and the negative commandments,
and the list of commandments by section), each part in three days at one
chapter a day, or one day at three. They also include The Order of Prayer
and the text of the Haggadah, as the published schedule does.

Tick **Follow** to follow a cycle from today. A followed cycle shows how
many days you marked learned out of the days since you started, and how
many are not marked. **Learned today** marks today; **Review later** makes
today's reading a review card in the review queue. The plans are saved in
`.lumen/learning.json` in your vault; nothing is sent anywhere, and Sefaria
opens only when you click a link. `{{learning}}` in the daily note template
writes one line per cycle with the same link.

pages.title: Import highlights (Kindle, Kobo, Readwise, Zotero)
pages.description: Bring your highlights from Kindle, Kobo, Readwise and Zotero into the vault, one note per book, with no duplicates when you import again.
pages.md:
Run `⌘K → "Import highlights (Kindle, Kobo, Readwise, Zotero)…"`, pick
where the highlights come from, then pick the file.

| From | What to pick |
|---|---|
| **Kindle** | `My Clippings.txt` in the Kindle's `documents` folder (connect it by USB). |
| **Kobo** | `KoboReader.sqlite` in the reader's hidden `.kobo` folder. |
| **Readwise** | The CSV export: Readwise → Export → CSV. |
| **Zotero** | Nothing to pick: Zotero 7 on this computer, desktop app only (see below). |

Every book or article gets a note, `Highlights/ — .md`. Each
highlight is a quote with:

- its place (page, location, or chapter and %);
- the date;
- tags and your note;
- for Zotero, a link that opens the annotation in its PDF.

Hebrew titles and texts work, file names included.

## Import again, any time

Importing the same file again only adds what's new:

- A highlight that's already in the note is left as it is, including any
  edits you made to it.
- If the app changed it (for example, you edited its note in Readwise),
  the entry is updated.
- A highlight you extended on the Kindle replaces the shorter one.
- The same passage from two apps (a Kindle highlight that Readwise also
  has) is **one** entry.
- Whatever you write in the note outside the highlights is kept.

Bookmarks, Kobo dog-ears and Zotero image or ink annotations have no text
and are left out; the import says how many.

Imported highlights appear in [All highlights](/workspace/highlights/)
under the kind **Imported**, and can be searched like the rest.

## Zotero

Zotero 7 serves your library to other apps on the same computer.

1. Turn it on in Zotero: **Settings → Advanced → "Allow other applications
   on this computer to communicate with Zotero"**.
2. With Zotero open, run the import in the **desktop app**. It reads your
   annotations from `127.0.0.1` (your own computer) and never from the
   cloud.

Zotero refuses requests from web pages, so in the browser the import
explains this instead.

Nothing is uploaded: the files are read on this device, and the only
request made is the desktop app's request to Zotero on this computer.

pages.title: All highlights
pages.description: Every highlight from PDFs, books and clipped pages in one place: search them, tag them, export them to a note with links back, or drag one into a note.
pages.md:
**Command palette → All highlights** lists every highlight in your vault:

- from **PDFs**, kept in `file.pdf.md` ([PDF reader](/workspace/pdf-reader/)),
- from **EPUB books**, kept in `book.epub.md` ([EPUB reader](/workspace/epub-reader/)),
- from **clipped pages**: passages marked `==like this==` in a note that was
  clipped from the web, or marked in [reading mode](/workspace/epub-reader/#reading-mode-for-clipped-pages).

## Find

Type in the search box to search the highlighted text, its note and its tags.
Case, spacing and Hebrew niqqud don't matter. Narrow the list by **kind**
(PDF, EPUB, clips), by **document** and by **tag**. Click a highlight to
open it: the reader opens at its page or chapter and flashes it.

## Tags

Type a tag under a PDF or EPUB highlight and press Enter. The tag is saved
with the highlight in its note (`file.pdf.md` or `book.epub.md`), as a W3C
Web Annotation tag, so it syncs with the note. **×** removes it. A clip's
highlights show the clip's own `tags:` from its front matter.

## Scan highlights from a printed book

In **All highlights**, choose **Scan a page**. Take a photo of the page with the phone's camera,
or drop or paste an image on the desktop.

- Lumen finds highlighter in **yellow, green, pink, orange or blue**, and **pen underlines**.
  The photo is checked by colour and by the shape of a drawn line, on this device.
- Only the marked lines go through the on-device OCR (Hebrew and English, mixed lines
  included). A word broken with a hyphen at the end of a line is joined again; a highlight
  that runs over several lines becomes one highlight.
- The page number is read from the page's header or footer when it is printed there; you can
  type or change it.
- Type the book's title and author (and its ISBN if you like; the check digit is verified).
  The highlights join that book's note in the `Highlights/` folder, with `p. N`, next to
  highlights imported from Kindle, Kobo, Readwise or Zotero for the same book.

The photo is **not kept** unless you tick **Keep the photo in the vault**; then it goes to
`Highlights/scans/`. Nothing is sent over the network: the detection and the OCR models are
part of the app.

## Export and drag

**Export to a note** writes the current list to a new note,
`Highlights <date>.md`: a section per document, each highlight as a quote with
its note, its tags and a link that opens it again.

Drag a highlight into a note: it drops as a quote with that link. Drag a PDF
highlight onto a canvas and it becomes a **highlight card**: the quote and
its page, linked to the exact place in the PDF. Opening the card's link
opens the reader at that page and flashes the highlight, found again by its
text even after the PDF's text layer changed or it was run through OCR. In
a `.canvas` (JSON Canvas) file the card is a file node with the highlight as
its subpath, as Obsidian Canvas keeps one. If you delete the highlight
later, the card stays on the canvas, dashed, and says the source was
deleted.

**Export with APA citations** (PDF highlights) writes the same note with a
Hebrew APA 7 citation after each quote, for example
"(כהן ואחרים, 2020, עמ׳ 14)", and a reference list at the end, Hebrew
sources before English ones. The citations follow the Bar-Ilan and Haifa
library guides (no comma before the last author's ו, "ואחרים" for three or
more) and are bidi isolates, so their brackets do not flip in a Hebrew
document. Each PDF's details come from your citation library (Zotero, or a
`.bib` / `.csl.json` file in the vault); a PDF it cannot match is asked
about once, and the answer is remembered on this device. The page is the
PDF page number; a book whose printed page numbers differ needs its page
labels, which this export does not read yet.

sections.heading: Find
sections.text: Type in the search box to search the highlighted text, its note and its tags. Case, spacing and Hebrew niqqud don't matter. Narrow the list by kind (PDF, EPUB, clips), by document and by tag . Click a highlight to open it: the reader opens at its page or chapter and flashes it.

sections.heading: Tags
sections.text: Type a tag under a PDF or EPUB highlight and press Enter. The tag is saved with the highlight in its note (file.pdf.md or book.epub.md), as a W3C Web Annotation tag, so it syncs with the note. × removes it. A clip's highlights show the clip's own tags: from its front matter.

sections.heading: Scan highlights from a printed book
sections.text: In All highlights , choose Scan a page . Take a photo of the page with the phone's camera, or drop or paste an image on the desktop. Lumen finds highlighter in yellow, green, pink, orange or blue , and pen underlines . The photo is checked by colour and by the shape of a drawn line, on this device. Only the marked lines go through the on-device OCR (Hebrew and English, mixed lines included). A word broken with a hyphen at the end of a line is joined again; a highlight that runs over several lines becomes one highlight. The page number is read from the page's header or footer when it is printed there; you can type or change it. Type the book's title and author (and its ISBN if you like; the check digit is verified). The highlights join that book's note in the Highlights/ folder, with p. N, next to highlights imported from Kindle, Kobo, Readwise or Zotero for the same book. The photo is not kept unless you tick Keep the photo in the vault ; then it goes to Highlights/scans/. Nothing is sent over the network: the detection and the OCR models are part of the app.

sections.heading: Export and drag
sections.text: Export to a note writes the current list to a new note, Highlights .md: a section per document, each highlight as a quote with its note, its tags and a link that opens it again. Drag a highlight into a note: it drops as a quote with that link. Drag a PDF highlight onto a canvas and it becomes a highlight card : the quote and its page, linked to the exact place in the PDF. Opening the card's link opens the reader at that page and flashes the highlight, found again by its text even after the PDF's text layer changed or it was run through OCR. In a .canvas (JSON Canvas) file the card is a file node with the highlight as its subpath, as Obsidian Canvas keeps one. If you delete the highlight later, the card stays on the canvas, dashed, and says the source was deleted. Export with APA citations (PDF highlights) writes the same note with a Hebrew APA 7 citation after each quote, for example "(כהן ואחרים, 2020, עמ׳ 14)", and a reference list at the end, Hebrew sources before English ones. The citations follow the Bar-Ilan and Haifa library guides (no comma before the last author's ו, "ואחרים" for three or more) and are bidi isolates, so their brackets do not flip in a Hebrew document. Each PDF's details come from your citation library (Zotero, or a .bib / .csl.json file in the vault); a PDF it cannot match is asked about once, and the answer is remembered on this device. The page is the PDF page number; a book whose printed page numbers differ needs its page labels, which this export does not read yet.

pages.title: Version history and undoing a delete
pages.description: Every note keeps its earlier versions, shared sessions included, in little space; a delete is undone with Ctrl+Z or from the trash; and the history panel shows whether the browser may clear your storage.
pages.md:
Lumen keeps what you wrote. Each note has a history of versions you can
read and restore, and a deleted note or folder goes to the trash, from
where one key brings it back.

## Version history

**⌘K → Version History** opens the open note's versions, newest first.
Pick one to preview it, with how many characters it differs by, then
**Restore this version**. Restoring keeps the current text as a version first, so a
restore can be undone too. **Keep a version now** saves one on demand.

A version is kept every couple of minutes while you type, on every save,
when you close the tab, before a git pull, before a restore, and every
ten minutes for the whole vault (also when the tab goes to the
background). Each version says why it was kept. Versions from a shared
editing session are kept in the same history, with who wrote them
("collab session · by …"), every five minutes and once more when the
session ends.

## How it stays small

Most versions are stored as the lines that changed from the version
before, compressed, with the full text every 20 versions. When the oldest
versions are removed, the oldest one left becomes a full text again, so
every remaining version still reads back exactly. A thousand versions of
a 6 KB note take about 6% of the space their full texts would.

Older copies that earlier versions of Lumen kept in a `backups/` folder
are moved into the history once, with their original times ("from old
backups"). The emptied folder goes to the trash. A `backups/` folder that
also holds your own notes is left where it is.

## Storage the browser may not clear

Browsers can clear a site's storage when the disk runs low, unless the
site's storage is persistent. The Version History panel shows which one
you have, how much is used (`X of Y`), and a **Keep my storage** button
that asks the browser to make it persistent. When storage passes 80%
full, Lumen tells you, and the oldest versions are removed first if it
runs out.

## Undoing a delete

A deleted note or folder goes to the trash for 30 days
(**⌘K → Trash…** restores it). Right after a delete, the message offers
**Undo**.

**⌘Z** / **Ctrl+Z** with the focus outside an editor (in the file tree, a
panel or the page) restores the last delete. Each press restores the one
before it, up to the last 20 deletes, and a delete of many files at once
counts as one. Inside the editor, a text field or the canvas, the same
key is their own undo. It also works on a Hebrew keyboard layout.

Before a note or folder is deleted, the unsaved edits of every open tab
inside it are saved, so restoring it brings back what you last typed.

pages.title: Import from other apps
pages.description: Bring notes from Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Apple Notes, Google Keep, Logseq, OneNote, Roam, Craft, Day One, Apple Journal, Samsung Notes, Airtable, Tomboy or any TextBundle app — into a new folder, with a report, undone in one click.
pages.md: **File → Import notes from another app…** (or the command palette) opens the import wizard. It never touches what you already have: everything goes into a new folder, `Imported/`, numbered when the name is taken. One click — **Undo the import** in the wizard, or the command **Undo the last import** later — takes it back. ## Three steps 1. **Pick the app** the notes come from. The wizard tells you how to export from it. 2. **Pick the export** — a file, several files, or a folder (or drop them on the wizard). Archives are opened, also archives inside archives (Notion zips its parts). If the files look like another app's export, the wizard says so and switches in one click. 3. **Check, then import.** Before anything is written you see how many notes, attachments and databases will come in, what will not and why, and how many internal links reach their note. ## What each app becomes | App | Export to pick | What it becomes | |---|---|---| | Obsidian | the vault folder, or a .zip of it | the vault as it is; `.obsidian/` and `.trash/` are left out | | Notion | Settings → Export → *Markdown & CSV* or *HTML*, the .zip as it came | names without Notion's ids; links follow the pages; **each database becomes a `.base` file** with the same columns, and each row a note whose properties are the row's cells (Yes/No, numbers and dates typed) | | Evernote | `.enex` files (one per notebook) | a folder per notebook; tasks, images and files in place (`_resources//`); tags, author, source URL, created and updated as properties; links between notes as `[[wikilinks]]`; encrypted parts are left out and reported | | Bear | a backup (`.bearbk`) or TextBundles | a note per bundle with its `assets/`; `::highlight::` → `==highlight==`, `#multi word tag#` → `#multi-word-tag`; trashed notes left out | | Apple Notes | its own database: the folder `~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.apple.notes` (or `NoteStore.sqlite` alone); or HTML or Markdown from an exporter app | from the database: a note per note in its folder, with created/modified dates; titles, headings, bold, italic, strikethrough, links, lists, checklists, code and quotes; images and files from `Media/`; locked notes and Recently Deleted left out, with the reason. From HTML: a note per page; images inside the HTML (`data:` URIs) become files; links between pages follow | | Google Keep | Google Takeout (Keep only), the .zip | checklists as tasks; labels as tags; colour and pin as properties; archived notes in `Archive/`; trashed notes left out | | Logseq | the graph folder, or a .zip | page properties as frontmatter; `TODO`/`DONE` as tasks; block references `((id))` and `{{embed}}` as `[[Page#^id]]` / `![[…]]`; journals named by date (`2024-01-31`); `a___b` pages as folders | | OneNote | pages or sections saved as *Single File Web Page* (`.mht`) | a note per page, its images and attached files next to it | | Roam Research | ⋯ → *Export All* → *JSON*: the `.json`, or the .zip as it came | a note per page; the blocks stay an outline (a heading block becomes a heading, `{{table}}` a table); `Name:: value` at the top of a page becomes a property; a block something refers to gets a `^id` and `((uid))`, `{{embed: ((uid))}}`, `[text](((uid)))` become `![[Page#^id]]` / `[[Page#^id\|text]]`; daily notes go to `journal/2021-01-02.md` and every link follows; `a/b` pages become folders; files Roam keeps on its servers stay links (nothing is downloaded) and the report says so | | Craft | *Export* → *Markdown* (or *TextBundle*), the .zip or the folder | a note per document, images next to it; `craftdocs://` links to a document of the export become `[[wikilinks]]`, and to a block `[[Document#^id]]` when the export carries the block's id; a link to something not in the export keeps its text and is reported; `` → `==…==` | | TextBundle | `.textbundle` folders or `.textpack` files (Ulysses, iA Writer and other editors), or a .zip of them | a note per bundle, named after it, its `assets/` in `assets//` with every link (Markdown or ``) following; an asset no link points at is listed at the end of the note, so none is lost; the app that wrote it as the property `source` | | Day One | *File → Export → JSON*, the .zip as it came | a note per entry in `//`; photos, videos, audio and PDFs (by their MD5) where the entry shows them, the rest listed below it; place, `coordinates` (shown on the map), weather, tags, star and dates as properties; a file the export lacks is reported | | Apple Journal | the exported folder (`Entries/`, `Resources/`), or a .zip | a note per entry, dated from its header (English or Hebrew); the prompt as a quote; photos and audio embedded; place, state of mind, activity, contact and media as properties | | Samsung Notes | notes shared as *Text file* or *PDF file* | a text note per file (☑ / □ become tasks); a PDF gets a note that shows it; Samsung's own `.sdocx` is reported (share as text or PDF instead) | | Airtable | each table's *Download CSV*, picked together; or a base saved from Airtable's API as JSON | a folder per table with a note per record and a `.base` that shows them; numbers and checkboxes typed, multiple selects as lists, a linked record as a `[[link]]`; attachments stay links to Airtable (nothing is fetched) | | Tomboy / Gnote | the notes folder, or its `.note` files | a note per note; notebooks as folders; bold, italic, strikethrough, highlight, monospace, links; lists, and tasks in a TODO note; a template to `Templates/` | Dates are kept as the properties `created` and `updated` (a browser cannot set a file's own dates). Hebrew names — files, folders, tags, properties — stay as they are; only characters a file system refuses are replaced. ## Other formats, through your Pandoc (desktop) If [Pandoc](https://pandoc.org) 2.15 or later is installed on the computer, the wizard offers **Pandoc** for the formats Lumen has no importer of its own for: DocBook, MediaWiki, Jira, OPML, txt2tags, DokuWiki, Textile, Creole, TWiki, TikiWiki, Vimwiki, Muse, FictionBook, man pages, Haddock and POD. Lumen does not include Pandoc (it is GPL software): it runs the copy you installed, with `--sandbox` (it reads the one file and writes the result, nothing else, no network) and a fixed set of options, and each run is listed in the privacy ledger. Without Pandoc, and in the browser, the choice is not shown. ## The report The last step shows what came in, what did not and why (the app's own settings, its trash, a second copy of a file, a format the app cannot convert, a damaged file), notes that came with something missing (an attachment the export does not have, an encrypted part, no dates), and links that point at nothing. **Save the report as a note** puts it in the import's folder (undo takes it back too). ## Undo Undo deletes exactly what the import wrote: its folder, and `Imported/` when the import made it. The vault is then the same, byte for byte, as before the import. If you changed something in the folder after the import, undo moves the folder to the trash instead, so nothing of yours is lost. ## Limits - Apple Notes: quit Notes before picking its folder. Changes Notes has not yet written into `NoteStore.sqlite` (its `-wal` file) are not read, and the report says so. Tables, drawings and scans in a note are not converted yet; the report lists each one. Locked notes need unlocking in Notes first. - OneNote's own `.one` files cannot be read; export pages or sections as `.mht`. A direct import through Microsoft Graph (sign in, read only: `Notes.Read`) needs an app registered with Microsoft: the deployment can name one in `/lumen-runtime.json` (`{"onenote": {"clientId": "…"}}`), or you can register your own free app in Microsoft Entra and paste its client ID into the wizard (it stays in this browser). The sign-in token stays in memory and is sent only to graph.microsoft.com. With a client ID, picking OneNote shows **Sign in to Microsoft and import from OneNote**: after the sign-in the wizard reads every notebook, section group and page, and shows the usual review before anything is written. - Notion's links to a block (`#…` after a page) go to the page: the block ids do not survive the export. ## How it is checked `src/__tests__/importWizard.test.ts` imports one golden export per app (`src/__tests__/fixtures/import/exports.ts`): 0 attachments lost, at least 98 % of internal links resolved, the Notion database as a `.base` with the same columns and rows, and an undo that gives back the same vault hash. `e2e/import-wizard.spec.ts` runs the wizard in the browser. Roam, Craft and TextBundle have their own tests (`importRoam`, `importCraft`, `importTextbundle`), as do Day One, Apple Journal, Samsung Notes, Tomboy and Airtable (`importDayOne`, `importJournal`, `importAirtable`), and `npm run import:diff` with no folders converts Obsidian Importer's own test exports (Keep, Roam, TextBundle, Tomboy, Apple Journal, Airtable, CSV) and compares lumen-md's output with the importer's recorded output, metric by metric. The golden exports are written from each app's documented format; real exports from the apps are the owner's check.

pages.title: Israeli time
pages.description: A Sunday–Thursday work week, the Hebrew date next to dates, and deadlines that move off Shabbat and chagim with a note saying why.
pages.md:
Lumen's calendar knows the Israeli week and the Jewish holidays (from its own
[Hebrew calendar](/workspace/hebrew-calendar/)). Nothing here rewrites a note: a moved
deadline is a suggestion shown next to the date you wrote.

## Settings

Open the calendar under the file tree and click its settings button.

| Setting | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| Work week | Sunday–Thursday when holidays are as in Israel, else Monday–Friday | In a Sunday–Thursday week Friday and Shabbat are the weekend; in a Monday–Friday week, Shabbat and Sunday. The calendar draws days off in a muted colour. |
| Hebrew dates | On for a Hebrew interface | The Hebrew date next to dates in a note's properties and in database views: `א׳ בתשרי תשפ״ז` in Hebrew, `1 Tishri 5787` otherwise. |
| A deadline on Shabbat or a chag | Suggest the next working day | Or the previous working day, or don't move it (only say why). |

The calendar starts the week on Sunday for Hebrew (and English), and on Monday for
French, German and Russian, as each language's own calendar does.

## Which days are off

- **Shabbat**, and the weekend of your work week.
- **Every yom tov:** Rosh Hashana (two days), Yom Kippur, the first day of Sukkot, Shemini
  Atzeret, the first and seventh days of Pesach and Shavuot. In the diaspora, the second
  days too. These are the Jewish rest days of the Hours of Work and Rest Law, 1951 (§18A).
- **Yom HaAtzmaut**, in Israel: a statutory holiday (Independence Day Law, 1949), on the
  day the government rules set (moved off Friday, Shabbat and Monday).

These days are working days, but get a note: **erev chag** (often a short day),
**Chol HaMoed** (many offices close), **fasts** (Tzom Gedaliah, 17 Tammuz, Tisha B'Av…),
**Yom HaZikaron** and **Yom HaShoah**.

## Deadlines

A **deadline** is a property named `due`, `deadline`, `due_date`, `יעד`, `תאריך יעד`,
`דדליין` or `מועד אחרון`. If it falls on a day off, you get a note:

> due: 2026-09-12 (א׳ בתשרי תשפ״ז) ⚠ Falls on Shabbat · Rosh Hashana I: suggested 2026-09-14 (Tzom Gedaliah)

Moving to the **next** working day is how Israeli law counts a period whose last day is a
day of rest (Interpretation Law, 1981, §10). Choose **previous** if you'd rather finish
before the chag.

### In a database view

Name the deadline column in the `database` block:

````md
```database
source: projects/
view: table
fields: [status, due]
deadline: due        # moved off Shabbat / chag, working days left
hebrewDate: true     # optional: overrides the setting for this block
```
````

The deadline column shows the date, the Hebrew date, the suggested working day when it
moves, and **working days left** (or overdue), counted over your work week and the
holidays. In the **calendar** view, every day has its Hebrew date and holidays, and each

pages.title: Jewish sources from Sefaria
pages.description: Quote a verse, a mishnah or a Talmud folio by its reference, with each text's licence. Keep a copy for offline use, and see every note that cites the same verse.
pages.md:
Type a reference the way you write it, such as `בראשית א:א`, `ב״ר א, א`,
`שמות כ׳ ג׳`, `Gen. 1:1-3` or `ברכות ב.`. Lumen brings the text from
[Sefaria](https://www.sefaria.org), the open library of Jewish texts, with
its niqqud and cantillation as they are.

## Quote a source

1. Select the reference in the source editor, or put the cursor on its line.
2. Open the command palette (⌘K) and run **Insert a source from Sefaria…**.
   With nothing selected, Lumen asks for the reference.
3. **Confirm the lookup.** The question says exactly what is sent: only the
   reference (for example `Genesis 1:1`), nothing from your notes.

The quote replaces the reference:

```markdown
> **[[Genesis.1.1|בראשית א׳:א׳]]**
>
> בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית בָּרָ֣א אֱלֹהִ֑ים …
>
> — [Sefaria](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.1) · עברית: Miqra according to the Masorah ([CC-BY-SA](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)) · English: … (CC-BY-NC) — link only
```

Every version's title and licence are written next to it. The link
`[[Genesis.1.1|…]]` makes the verse a node in the graph.

## Licences: what is copied and what is only linked

Sefaria gives each version of a text, in each language, its own licence.
Lumen reads that licence from Sefaria's own data and follows it:

| Licence | In your note | In the offline copy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public Domain, CC0 | the text | the text |
| CC-BY, CC-BY-SA | the text, with its credit and licence | the text, with its credit and licence |
| CC-BY-NC, CC-BY-NC-SA, CC-BY-NC-ND | a link only | not stored |
| Copyright, or no licence noted | a link only | not stored |

**Non-commercial licences count as not free.** A note travels: it syncs,
gets published and gets exported, and Lumen cannot know what it will be used
for. **"No licence noted" means Sefaria has not checked the copyright yet.**
A non-free text is dropped as soon as Sefaria's answer is read. It never
reaches a note, the vault or a cache.

## Keep a copy for offline use

Saving is your choice and never automatic. Use the **Save for offline**
button on the message after a quote, or run **Save this source for offline**.
The copy goes to `Sources/Sefaria/.md`:

- **its frontmatter** records every version's title, licence, licence link and
  source, and whether it was copied;
- **its body** holds the free texts only.

Once a source is saved, quoting it again uses the copy: no request, no
question, and it works with no network at all.

## My notes on this verse

Put the cursor on a reference, or open a saved source note, and run **My notes
on this verse**. Lumen lists every note that cites the verse, through a wiki
link (`[[בראשית א:א]]`, `[[Genesis.1.1]]`) or a Sefaria link. The search
reads your vault on this device and sends nothing.

## Privacy

A lookup sends only the reference to `www.sefaria.org`. The privacy ledger
lists each lookup as a consented request, and the cloud-routes table lists it
as `sefaria-texts`. The *local only* policy doesn't block a lookup you
confirmed, the same way it treats a diagram you chose to send.

## What is recognised

- **Books:**
  - the Tanakh, with Hebrew and English names and the usual abbreviations
    (`בר׳`, `ש״א`, `Gen.`, `1 Sam`);
  - Midrash Rabbah (`ב״ר`, `שמו״ר` …);
  - the Mishnah (`משנה ברכות א:א`, `אבות א:א`);
  - the Babylonian Talmud (`ברכות ב.`, `ב״מ נט:`, `Berakhot 2a`).
- **Numbers** can be Hebrew numerals, with or without geresh or gershayim
  (`קי״ט`, `טו`), or digits. A range is written `א:א-ג`.
- **Not supported yet:** commentaries (`רש״י על בראשית א:א`), the Jerusalem
  Talmud, halakhic codes, and ranges that cross chapters.

## About Sefaria

Lumen uses Sefaria's public texts API, which needs no key. "Sefaria" is a
trademark of Sefaria; Lumen is not made or endorsed by Sefaria.

pages.title: JSON Canvas (Obsidian .canvas)
pages.description: Open Obsidian canvases in Lumen's Excalidraw canvas and write them back as .canvas files. JSON Canvas is an open, MIT-licensed format.
pages.md:
[JSON Canvas](https://jsoncanvas.org) is the open format Obsidian uses for its
canvases (`.canvas` files, spec 1.0, MIT licensed). Lumen's
[canvas](/workspace/canvas/) reads and writes it. Everything runs on your device.

## Import

- **Import .canvas** in the canvas bar: pick a `.canvas` file. It becomes a new
  canvas, `canvases/<name>.excalidraw`, and opens. If that name is taken, you
  get `<name>-2`, `<name>-3` and so on, and nothing is overwritten.
- A `.canvas` file already in the vault's `canvases/` folder (for example from
  a synced Obsidian vault) is listed in the picker with a **Convert** button,
  like old tldraw canvases. The `.canvas` file stays as it was.

## Export

**Export .canvas** writes the open canvas to `canvases/<name>.canvas`, next to
its `.excalidraw` file, byte for byte in Obsidian's own layout (tabs, one
node or edge per line, no space after a colon). A canvas from Obsidian that
you import and export without edits comes back byte-identical.
Exporting again replaces that `.canvas` file. The `.excalidraw` file is not
touched.

## How it maps

| JSON Canvas | Excalidraw |
|---|---|
| Text node (Markdown) | Rectangle with the text inside (shown as written, not rendered) |
| File node (`file`, `subpath`) | Rectangle showing the path, with the path as the element's link |
| Link node (`url`) | Rectangle showing the URL, with the URL as the element's link |
| Group (`label`) | Frame with the label as its name. Nodes inside it belong to the frame (to the smallest one, since Excalidraw frames don't nest) |
| Edge (`fromSide`/`toSide`, `fromEnd`/`toEnd`, `label`) | Arrow bound to both nodes at those sides, with arrowheads per end and the label on the arrow |
| Colour: preset `1`–`6` or hex | Stroke colour (the presets as Obsidian draws them: red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, purple) |

**Round trip.** Each element keeps the node or edge it came from, so a canvas
that is imported and exported without edits comes back the same, including
what Excalidraw has no place for: a file's subpath, a group's background, and
fields added by other apps. Edits are written back. Moved or resized nodes,
changed text, a changed link (`Notes/Plan.md#Goals` → `file` + `subpath`),
recoloured elements and arrows that now connect different nodes are all
exported.

**Drawn in Excalidraw.** Rectangles, ellipses and diamonds become text nodes
(with the text inside them), a shape with a link becomes a link or file node,
free text becomes a text node, frames become groups, and arrows bound to two
of those become edges. Images, free-hand strokes, lines and arrows not
connected at both ends have no JSON Canvas form. They are left out of the
`.canvas` file, the export says how many, and they stay in the
`.excalidraw` canvas.

pages.title: Laws and Knesset records
pages.description: Cite a law by its name, a bill and a committee protocol from the Knesset's open data, keep laws for offline use, and ask the laws you saved.
pages.md:
Write a law's name the way you usually do: `חוק הגנת הפרטיות`,
`חוק הגנת הפרטיות, התשמ״א-1981`, `לחוק הגנת הפרטיות`, `[[חוק:חופש המידע]]`,
or a Basic Law as `חוק יסוד: כבוד האדם וחירותו` or `ח״י: כבוד האדם וחירותו`.
Lumen finds the law in the Knesset's public records (its OData service) and
inserts a citation with a link to the record.

## Turn it on

Knesset sources start **off**. The first time you use one of the commands,
Lumen asks to turn them on. You can turn them off again in **Open sources**.

## Cite a law

1. Put the cursor on a line that names a law, or select the name.
2. Open the command palette and choose **Cite a law (Knesset)…**.
3. Lumen asks before it sends anything. Only the name is sent to
   `knesset.gov.il`, never your note. The request is listed in the
   privacy ledger.
4. When more than one law matches, pick one.

The toast offers **Save for offline**. A saved law is a note in
`Sources/Knesset/Laws/` with its source, the date it was retrieved and its
rights in the frontmatter. The next time you cite it, Lumen finds it there
and sends nothing, online or not.

## Rights

Section 6 of the Copyright Act, 2007 says there is no copyright in laws,
regulations, Knesset records (דברי הכנסת) and judicial decisions. So a
saved law may hold the full text: paste it under `## נוסח`. Documents
attached to a session, such as legal opinions and presentations, are not
Knesset records, so Lumen keeps only their link.

## Bills

**Cite a bill (Knesset)…** searches bills by a word of their name, saves the
one you pick in `Sources/Knesset/Bills/` and links to it.

## Committee protocols

Open a committee protocol's text in Lumen, select the words, and choose
**Quote from this committee protocol**. The quote gets the speaker, the
session date and the page, written after the Uniform Citation Rules, for
example: `פרוטוקול ישיבה מס' 12 של ועדת החוקה, חוק ומשפט, הכנסת ה-25, 2 (3.1.2023)`.
Nothing is sent: the details come from the protocol's first lines.

## Ask the law

**Ask the law…** searches the sections of the laws you saved, on this
device, and inserts the section you pick, quoted word for word with its
citation. That is a **quote from the law, not a verified answer**: nothing
checks that the section answers your question, and the note says so.

With a model on this device (Ollama, or the in-browser model), Lumen also
writes a short answer from that one section, and a critic checks it
against the section's text. The answer is marked verified only when the
critic finds the section supports it. An answer with a number the section
doesn't contain (a deadline, an amount) is never verified, whatever the
model says. Without a local model there is no answer and nothing is
verified, only the quote. The cloud is never used for this.

## What is not here yet

- Court decisions (a separate study of the Judiciary's terms comes first).
- Fetching a law's consolidated text: the Knesset's OData service has the
  law's details, not its text, so you paste the text yourself.

pages.title: Large vaults and long notes
pages.description: How Lumen stays fast with 10,000 notes and with a single 2 MB note — and how that is measured.
pages.md:
Lumen is built to stay responsive with a vault of **10,000 notes** and with a
single note of **2 MB** (plan 8.4). Nothing needs to be switched on; this page
explains what happens and what to expect.

## A vault with thousands of notes

- **The index lives in a Web Worker.** Search (`⇧⌘F`), backlinks and the tags
  panel read one shared index of your notes. It is built once, in a
  background worker, so a query over 10,000 notes never blocks typing.
  Hebrew search (niqqud, final letters and prefix letters folded) is prepared
  when a note is indexed, not on every query.
- **A save re-indexes only that note.** After the first build, saving a note
  re-reads that note alone; renaming or deleting a note or a folder moves or
  drops its entries without reading anything. When files change behind
  Lumen's back (another tab, a folder edited elsewhere), the index re-lists
  the vault and re-reads only the files whose modification time changed.
- **The file tree and the index share one listing** of the vault after a
  structural change.
- **Big vaults open with folders collapsed.** With more than 1,000 notes the
  file tree starts with its folders closed (the folders of the open note stay
  open), so opening the vault does not render 10,000 rows.

## A very long note

From 50,000 characters on, three things change — the result on screen is the
same:

- **The outline** re-parses only the blocks that changed (a paragraph, a list,
  a code block). Opening or closing a code fence, or changing a reference
  definition (`[label]: url`), re-parses what it affects.
- **The preview** is rendered block by block. After an edit only the changed
  blocks are rendered again, and rendering pauses every few milliseconds so
  the editor stays fluid. The blocks you can see come first; the rest of the
  note fills in while the browser is idle, and a part you scroll to jumps the
  queue. Until a block is ready it holds its place with a blank of about its
  height, so the page does not jump, and a link to a heading in it waits for
  it. A note with footnotes, reference definitions or suggestions
  (CriticMarkup) is rendered in one pass, as before.

## Rendering off the main thread

The preview of every note — Markdown parsing, code highlighting (Shiki) and
math (KaTeX) — is worked out in a background worker, so typing is never
held up by it. Link hover cards are made there too. Code blocks and formulas
that did not change are not highlighted or typeset again. Without a worker
(an old browser, or one that blocks it) the same work runs in the page, and
the result is the same.
- **The word count** in the status bar, and keeping a copy of the open note
  in the browser's storage for the next session, happen when you pause
  typing rather than on every keystroke.

## Targets and how they are checked

| What | Target | Checked by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open the app with 10,000 notes | < 1 s | `e2e/perf-vault.spec.ts` (production build) |
| Save → index updated | < 50 ms | `e2e/perf-vault.spec.ts`, `src/__tests__/vaultWorker.test.ts` |
| Search 10,000 notes | < 100 ms | `e2e/perf-vault.spec.ts`, `src/__tests__/vaultWorker.test.ts` |
| Typing in a 2 MB note | < 16 ms per keystroke | `e2e/perf-vault.spec.ts` (`@nightly`) |

The unit tests count work rather than time it: a save reads one note and
re-indexes one note, a rename reads none, backlinks read only the linking
notes, a keystroke in a long note re-parses one block. The outline is
compared with the one-pass outline on random documents and random edits.

The 2 MB typing test runs every night (`.github/workflows/nightly-perf.yml`),
not on every pull request. To run it yourself against a production build:

```sh
npm run build
npx http-server dist -p 5180 -c-1 --cors &
PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL=http://localhost:5180 npx playwright test --project=perf
```

Each run attaches the measured numbers to the Playwright report as `perf`
annotations.

## Responsiveness budget

Load time is measured by Lighthouse; how fast each action answers is
measured separately (plan W1.22), in Chromium with the CPU slowed 4×, like a
mid-range phone:

| What | Budget |
| --- | --- |
| INP over 20 fixed interactions (palette, view modes, opening and switching notes, typing, a task checkbox, search, undo) | p75 < 100 ms |
| Key press → next frame, end of a 50 KB note | p95 < 16 ms |
| Key press → next frame, end of a 2 MB note | p95 < 33 ms |

```sh
npm run perf:inp          # measures (e2e/inp-budget.spec.ts), then gates
npm run perf:inp:gate -- --record   # also appends the run to reports/perf/inp-trend.jsonl
```

The run writes `reports/perf/inp-latest.json`. The gate compares it with
`reports/perf/inp-baseline.json` and fails when any of the three numbers is
10 % or more slower; the first run becomes the baseline
(`npm run perf:inp:gate -- --update` replaces it on purpose).

## Responsiveness on real devices

`npm run perf:responsiveness` measures both editors (source and WYSIWYG) on
a 10,000-note vault, against the production build (plan W6.45):

| Environment | Where | INP p75 budget |
|---|---|---|
| `desktop-chromium` | Desktop Chrome, CPU as is | < 100 ms |
| `mid-phone-emulated` | Pixel 7 emulation, CPU 4× slower | < 200 ms |
| `real-device-*` | real Pixel and iPhone on BrowserStack (`perf:responsiveness -- browserstack`) | < 200 ms |

Keypress → paint p95 must stay under 16 ms in a 50 KB note and under 33 ms
in a 2 MB note, everywhere. Safari has no Event Timing API, so on an iPhone
only keypress → paint is measured; INP shows as "not measured" there,
never as 0.

The related-notes panel is open during the whole measurement, because it
re-ranks after every pause in typing. A build without the panel still runs,
but its run says `relatedPanel: false`, it scores no board number, and it is
never compared with a baseline taken with the panel. To make a new baseline,
run `node scripts/perf/responsiveness.mjs gate --update`.

Each environment has its own baseline in `reports/perf/baselines/<env>.json`.
The first run writes it; commit it. A later run fails when any number is
10 % or more slower than that baseline. The run also writes a signed
`lumen-metric` receipt to `reports/metrics/`, which the area board scores
(`perf.inp-p75-ms`, `perf.inp-p75-mid-phone-ms`, `perf.key2paint-p95-*`).
The nightly perf run and the verification factory run it every night.

## For developers

- `src/storage/vaultIndexCore.ts` — the index (pure, runs in the worker or in
  the page); `src/storage/vaultIndex.worker.ts` and
  `src/storage/vaultIndexProtocol.ts` — the worker and its messages;
  `src/storage/workspaceIndex.ts` — the main-thread side, fed by the
  VaultBackend's events (`watchVault`).
- `src/renderer/blocks.ts` — top-level blocks of a document, re-scanned only
  around an edit; `src/renderer/incrementalToc.ts` and
  `src/renderer/incrementalPreview.ts` build on it.
- `src/renderer/renderCore.ts` — the pipeline up to HAST (no React, no DOM);
  `src/renderer/render.worker.ts` and `src/renderer/renderWorkerCore.ts` — the
  render worker; `src/renderer/renderProtocol.ts` — its messages (a version
  per preview, so a newer render makes an older one stale);
  `src/renderer/renderClient.ts` — the page's side, with the fallback;
  `src/renderer/hastToReact.ts` — the one step that stays in the page.
  `src/renderer/viewport.ts` orders the blocks of a long note. Shiki and KaTeX
  keep their output per block (`src/renderer/blockCache.ts`,
  `src/renderer/math.ts`). Tests: `src/__tests__/renderWorker.test.ts` and
  `src/__tests__/viewportPreview.test.ts`.

  norms precomputed (`packVectors` in `src/ai/semanticSearch.ts`).

pages.title: Academic LaTeX export (Hebrew)
pages.description: Export a note as a LaTeX project — Hebrew right to left with babel, math, Pandoc-style [@key] citations from the vault's BibTeX, and images — that compiles with LuaLaTeX or XeLaTeX.
pages.md:
**Export LaTeX project (academic, Hebrew)…** in the command palette
downloads `<note>-latex.zip` with:

- `main.tex` — the note as an `article`: `#` becomes the title (or
  `title:` from the frontmatter), `##` sections, lists, quotes, tables,
  footnotes, code (left to right, verbatim), inline `$…$` and display
  `$$…$$` math as written;
- the reference list, in APA (the same formatter as Lumen's citations),
  each entry in its own language and direction;
- `references.bib` — the cited entries from every `.bib` in the vault, for
  a bibtex or biblatex style of your own;
- `images/` — the images the note shows;
- `README.txt` with the compile command.

Compile with `latexmk -lualatex main.tex` (recommended) or
`latexmk -xelatex main.tex`. Both work from the same preamble.

## PDF from LaTeX (desktop)

In the desktop app, **PDF from LaTeX (desktop, Tectonic)…** compiles the
same export into `<note>.pdf` with [Tectonic](https://tectonic-typesetting.github.io),
if you have installed it (`brew install tectonic`). Lumen does not bundle a TeX
engine. It finds `tectonic` on your `PATH`, in `/opt/homebrew/bin` or
`/usr/local/bin`, or at the path in `LUMEN_TECTONIC`. The project is compiled
in a temporary folder that is removed afterwards. Tectonic runs with
`--untrusted`, so the document can't run shell commands.

When TeX fails, Lumen lists its errors with their lines in `main.tex`
(`main.tex:7: Undefined control sequence.`), or the end of the log when TeX
gives no line. In the browser there is no compiler; export the project and
compile it yourself.

## Hebrew

The preamble uses **babel** with `\babelprovide[import, main]{hebrew}`
— `bidi=basic` under LuaLaTeX, which babel's maintainers recommend for
right-to-left text, and `bidi=default` under XeLaTeX. Polyglossia was not
chosen: under XeLaTeX it needs the separate `bidi` package, and babel
covers both engines with one preamble.

In a Hebrew paper every run of Latin text (a term, a name, `1–20` page
ranges, an e-mail) is wrapped in `\foreignlanguage{english}{…}`, so it
reads left to right with the right font and hyphenation; in an English
paper Hebrew runs get `\foreignlanguage{hebrew}{…}`. Math and code are
always left to right. The paper's language is decided by its letters.

Fonts: Frank Ruhl Libre or David Libre (SIL Open Font Licence, free from
Google Fonts) when installed, else Noto Serif Hebrew or FreeSerif; Latin
Modern for English.

## Citations

Pandoc's syntax, as in Lumen's citation dialog:

| In the note | In main.tex |
|---|---|
| `[@cohen2020]` | `\citep{cohen2020}` |
| `[see @knuth1984, p. 33]` | `\citep[see][p.~33]{knuth1984}` |
| `[@a; @b]` | `\citep{a,b}` |
| `@cohen2020 showed` | `\citet{cohen2020} showed` |

Only keys found in a `.bib` in the vault become citations (so an e-mail
address stays text); the toast lists cited keys that are missing.

## How it was checked

`src/__tests__/latexAcademic.test.ts` turns ten golden notes in
`src/__tests__/fixtures/latex/` (Hebrew, English, mixed runs, inline and
display math, citations, lists and quotes, a table, footnotes and links,
code and special characters, an English paper with Hebrew) into exactly the
`.tex` beside each. All ten compiled with XeLaTeX (TeX Live 2023) with no
errors and no missing characters; the PDFs read right to left.

pages.title: Links, embeds and block references
pages.description: Link notes with [[ and its completion, preview a link by hovering, turn plain mentions into links, embed a note or one of its sections, and link to a single paragraph with ^id.
pages.md:
Notes link to each other with `[[Note name]]`, as in Obsidian. The links
work in the source editor, in the preview and in WYSIWYG, and they keep
working when a note is renamed or moved.

## Link completion

Type `[[` and a list of matching notes opens. It matches the way the vault
names notes: case, niqqud, final letters and spaces don't matter, so
`[[שלום` finds `שָׁלוֹם.md`. A name that two notes share is inserted as its
path.

| You type | The list offers |
|---|---|
| `[[que` | notes whose name, or an alias in their front matter (`aliases:`), matches |
| `[[Note#` | the headings of that note |
| `[[#` | the headings of the open note |
| `[[Note#^` | the block ids (`^id`) of that note |

Picking an alias inserts `[[Note|Alias]]`. When no note has exactly the
name you typed, the last entry is **Create note «…»**: it writes
`Name.md` with a `# Name` heading and never overwrites an existing file.
**↑** / **↓** move, **Enter** or **Tab** inserts, **Esc** closes the list.
Inside code the list stays closed.

## Hover preview

In the preview, point at a `[[link]]` for a moment, or move the keyboard
focus to it, and a card shows the first 20 lines of the note, rendered.
`[[Note#Heading]]` starts the card at that heading, and `[[Note#^id]]`
shows that block. **Esc**, moving away or leaving the link hides it. In
the source editor the same card opens when the mouse rests on a link. A
link to a note that doesn't exist yet says so instead.

## Unlinked mentions

The backlinks panel (**⌘K → Toggle backlinks**) lists the notes that link
here, and below them **Unlinked mentions**: notes that write this note's
title as plain text. Each has a **Link** button that turns that mention
into `[[Title]]`, or `[[Title|as written]]` when the case differs.

Only whole words count. A Hebrew prefix (ו, ה, ב, ל, מ, ש, כ, וב, של) stays
outside the link, so `בתל אביב` becomes `ב[[תל אביב]]`. Text inside links,
URLs, code, front matter and HTML is never touched, and a note never
counts as mentioning itself. Mentions match the title, not the aliases.

## Embeds

`![[…]]` shows another note, or part of it, inside this one:

| Syntax | Shows |
|---|---|
| `![[Note]]` | the whole note, with a small link that opens it |
| `![[Note#Heading]]` | that section, up to the next heading of the same or a higher level |
| `![[Note#^id]]` | one block |
| `![[#Heading]]` | a section of the note you are in |
| `![[image.png]]`, `![[image.png\|300]]` | an image from the vault, optionally 300 px wide (`\|300x200` sets both sides) |
| `![[file.pdf]]` | a card that opens the PDF |

Embeds nest up to three levels. A note that embeds itself, directly or
through other notes, shows a notice instead of looping, and so do a
missing note and a missing section. When an embedded note changes, the
embed updates. A Hebrew note embedded in an English one keeps its own
direction.

## Block references

A paragraph or list item that ends with ` ^id` can be linked on its own:
`[[Note#^id]]` opens the note and scrolls to it, and `![[Note#^id]]`
embeds it. A table, quote or code block gets its id on a line of its own
right after it. The `^id` marker is hidden in the preview.

**⌘K → Copy link to block** does this for you in the source editor: it
gives the block at the cursor an id (six letters and digits, unique in
the note; a block that has one keeps it) and copies `[[Note#^id]]`. On a
heading it copies the heading's link. In WYSIWYG the command points you to
the source editor (**⌘1**).

## Renaming and moving

Renaming or moving a note rewrites every link to it, and keeps the
`#heading`, `#^id` and `|alias` parts. Moving an image rewrites only the
embeds that pointed at that file, not ones that open a file with the same
name in another folder. [Vault Doctor](/workspace/doctor/) reports links
to block ids that no longer exist.

pages.title: Literature review matrix
pages.description: One table of every PDF in the vault, with question, method, sample, findings and limitations, and each value backed by a quote verified on its page. Runs on this device.
pages.md:
`⌘K` → **Literature review from the vault's PDFs** reads every PDF in the
vault on this device. Scanned pages are read with OCR. It writes:

- **one note per paper** in `Literature review/`, with five fields as
  properties: question, method, sample, findings and limitations. Under each
  value are the quotes it came from, each with a link to its page and line;
- **`Literature review.base`**, which shows the notes as a table, one row per
  paper and one column per field (Obsidian Bases format). It has two views:
  **All papers** and **Verified only**, which lists only the papers where
  every field is verified.

## Argument map

Give notes `type: claim` (טענה) or `type: evidence` (מקור, a source), and
link them with `supports:`, `contradicts:` or `qualifies:` (each a list of
`[[links]]` to claims). Mark the end points with `conclusion: true`. An
`argument-map` block draws them:

```argument-map
folder: research/wages     # optional
```

- Sources sit in the first column (on the right in Hebrew), then the claims
  they lead to, then the conclusions. Green lines support, red dashed lines
  contradict, yellow dotted lines qualify.
- A claim that no source reaches through "supports" or "qualifies" is
  marked **no source**.
- "Show as a list" gives the same map as a nested list: each claim with the
  notes that support, contradict or qualify it. On the map, **Tab** to it,
  then the arrow keys go from note to note and **Enter** opens one.
- "Save as a canvas" writes the map to `canvases/` as a JSON Canvas (opens
  in Obsidian) and as an Excalidraw drawing.
- The two types are built in, so they show in the type list, the type's
  Base and the properties form like your own types.

## No value without a quote

For each field, the passages that search finds go to the local model. The
model answers with quotes copied from those passages. Each quote is then
looked up in its passage and located on its page:

- A value is kept only when at least one of its quotes is found.
- Quotes that were made up, or that cite the wrong passage, are dropped. If
  none is left, the field shows "No value with a verified quote" instead of
  a guess.

The model is the local one in AI settings (Ollama or the browser model). A
cloud model is used only if your AI policy allows it.

## Competing hypotheses (ACH)

An `ach` block weighs evidence against competing explanations, the way
Richards Heuer's Analysis of Competing Hypotheses does:

```ach
title: Who leaked the report?
hypotheses:
  H1: Someone inside
  H2: A contractor
evidence:
  - text: The file names an office laptop
    weight: 3
    marks: { H1: CC, H2: I }
  - text: The contractor's own blog post
    deceptive: true
    marks: { H1: N, H2: C }
```

- Each mark is **CC** (very consistent), **C**, **N** (neutral; an empty
  cell is N), **I** (inconsistent) or **II**; `++ + 0 - --` work too. A
  weight is a whole number (default 1).
- Hypotheses are ranked by the **least** weighted inconsistency
  (I = 1, II = 2 per weight): evidence rules hypotheses out more than it
  proves them. Ties go to the most consistency.
- The block also says which rows don't tell the hypotheses apart, which
  single row the verdict rests on (a linchpin), and whether the leader
  holds without the rows marked `deceptive`.
- "Copy as a table" copies the matrix as a Markdown table. It is a research
  instrument, not a verdict.

## How it is measured

`eval/probes/lit-review.json` has five short papers (English and Hebrew).
For each field it records the right page and a phrase from it.

- `src/__tests__/litReview.test.ts` runs retrieval and verification on
  them with a stand-in model. Retrieval finds the right passage for 24 of
  the 25 fields, and every kept citation is on the right page. It also
  checks that a model that makes quotes up has nothing kept.
- `npm run eval:lit-review` runs the real model and reports the share of
  fields that are right.
- The acceptance set is 20 real papers, which the owner provides in the same
  file format. The plan's targets: 85% of fields right, every citation on the
  right page.

pages.title: Mail and Google Takeout into notes
pages.description: Import .eml and .mbox mail and a Google Takeout archive (Keep, Docs) into notes, from files only, with Hebrew mail in every old encoding.
pages.md:
**⌘K → Import mail (.eml, .mbox) or Google Takeout…** reads mail and Google
data **from files only**. No account is connected and nothing leaves this
device.

## What you can pick

| Source | File |
|---|---|
| Single messages | `.eml`, saved from any mail app |
| Mailboxes | `.mbox`: Gmail's Takeout, Thunderbird, Apple Mail |
| Google Takeout | the `takeout-….zip`, with **Mail** (an `.mbox` with Gmail labels), **Keep** and **Drive** |

When the mailbox has Gmail labels, Lumen asks which label to import, or all
of them. Each label is shown with its message count.

## What you get

Everything goes into new folders in `Imported/`, and nothing existing is
overwritten:

- **Mail**: one note per **thread**, linked by `Message-ID`, `In-Reply-To`
  and `References`. Without those headers, the subject is used, minus `Re:`,
  `Fwd:`, `השב:` and `הועבר:`. Messages run oldest first, each under the
  sender and date, with To/Cc. Attachments are copied to `attachments/`:
  pictures are shown in place, other files linked. The frontmatter holds the
  subject, participants, first and last date, and labels.
- **Google Keep**: one note per Keep note. You get the text, the checklist
  as `- [ ]` / `- [x]`, labels as tags, created and edited times, pinned and
  archived, the attachments and the links. Notes in Keep's trash are left
  out, and the report says how many.
- **Google Docs**: Takeout exports Docs as `.docx` by default, and they
  become Markdown. `.odt`, `.rtf`, `.html`, `.txt` and `.md` work too. Any
  other Drive file is copied as it is, in its folder.

The folders are marked as outside content, so AI agents treat their text as
other people's words.

## Hebrew mail in old encodings

Mail from older Israeli systems often isn't UTF-8. Lumen reads:

- **windows-1255** and **ISO-8859-8-I**: Hebrew in logical order, as typed.
- **ISO-8859-8**: in MIME this label means **visual** order. Each line is
  stored as it looks on a left-to-right screen, so the Hebrew reads
  backwards (RFC 1555 and the Hebrew-mail draft that followed it). Lumen
  turns those lines around and keeps English words, numbers and links in
  their own order. Many mail apps also put normal, logical text under this
  label. Lumen tells the two apart by the final letters (ך ם ן ף ץ): they end
  words in logical text and start them in visual text. A plain כ מ נ פ צ at
  the end of a word is another sign of visual text.
- Encoded-words in subjects and names (`=?windows-1255?B?…?=`, `?Q?`, in
  any charset), file names in the `filename*=utf-8''…` form, and raw 8-bit
  headers.

## Large mailboxes

A 5,000-message mbox is read and turned into notes in about a second (measured
in the test suite; the plan's limit is 2 minutes). The whole file is read into memory, so a Takeout mbox of several GB
is best split by label in Takeout first (one `.mbox` per label).

pages.title: Audio and video with a transcript
pages.description: Embed a recording, read its WebVTT or SRT transcript beside the player, and click a line to jump there.
pages.md:
Write `![[rec.m4a]]` (or `.mp3`, `.wav`, `.ogg`, `.webm`, `.mp4`, `.mov`…)
in a note to embed a recording from your vault.

- **The transcript beside the player.** If a transcript file sits next to
  the recording under its full name (`rec.m4a.vtt`, in
  [WebVTT](https://www.w3.org/TR/webvtt1/), or `rec.m4a.srt`) or under its
  name without the extension (`rec.vtt`, `rec.srt`), its lines appear under
  the player with their times and speakers. The full name is tried first.
- **Click a line** to play from that moment. The line being spoken is
  marked as it plays.
- **Video:** the same track is used as captions.

## Where transcripts come from

**Transcribe a meeting** already writes the timed transcript into the
note. It also proposes it as `rec.m4a.vtt` and `rec.m4a.srt` next to the
audio, so the embed, a video player or a subtitle editor can use it. The
two files wait in the review panel, like every change an AI feature makes,
and are written only when you approve them; a track that is already there
(one you corrected by hand, say) is shown there as the file being changed,
and is kept if you changed it again in the meantime. The names keep the
recording's extension, so `meeting.m4a` and `meeting.wav` never share a
track, and a second recording with the same name on the same day is kept as
`…-2.m4a` rather than over the first. Nothing is transcribed again. A `.vtt`
or `.srt` from another app works the same way.

The files are standard WebVTT and SubRip:
- WebVTT starts with `WEBVTT`.
- Each cue has a `start --> end` timing in order.
- Speakers are `<v Name>` voice spans.
- `&`, `<` and `>` are escaped.

pages.title: The vault in a folder on your phone
pages.description: In the iOS and Android apps, keep the vault in a real folder — the Files app on iOS, a folder you pick on Android — and see edits made there.
pages.md:
In the phone app the vault starts in the app's private storage. **Command
palette → Move the vault to a folder…** puts it in a real folder on the
phone, where other apps can open and edit the notes:

| | Where the vault goes |
|---|---|
| **iOS** | The app's Documents folder. In the **Files** app it is *On My iPhone › Lumen*; other apps can open and edit the notes in place. |
| **Android** | A folder you pick in the system's folder picker (any folder on the phone or the SD card). Lumen keeps the permission across restarts. If the app was built without Lumen's folder plugin, the app's own folder on the device is used instead. |

The move copies every note, reads each copy back and compares it, and only
then switches; the app storage is kept as it was. **Open a folder as the
vault…** uses a folder that already has notes, without copying.

## Edits made in other apps

Lumen checks the folder every few seconds while it is open, and at once
when you come back to it (for example from the Files app). A changed note
updates in Lumen; if you changed the same note in Lumen at the same time,
you get the conflict dialog and nothing is lost (see *Changes made outside
Lumen*).

## When the folder is gone

On Android the permission can be taken back in the system settings, or the
folder can be deleted. Lumen then shows the vault as **disconnected** and
reads and writes nothing until you pick the folder again (**Reconnect**).

## Status

The app side is complete and tested against both phone file APIs. The
native pieces are listed in `mobile/README.md` in the repository: the
official `@capacitor/filesystem` plugin (iOS and the Android fallback) and
Lumen's small Android folder plugin; checks on real devices are still open.

pages.title: Notion's formulas in Bases
pages.description: Notion's formula functions (dates, text, numbers, lists with current and index, lookups through relations) inside .base formulas and filters, plus two for Hebrew.
pages.md:
A `.base` formula or filter can use Notion's formula functions next to
Obsidian's own, so a database brought over from Notion keeps its formulas.
Where a name is already an Obsidian function (`if`, `min`, `max`, `empty`,
`now`, `today`, `link`, `date`, `list`, `number`), Obsidian's meaning stays,
because a `.base` file must mean in Lumen what it means in Obsidian.

## The functions

| Group | Functions |
|---|---|
| Logic | `ifs`, `let`, `lets`, `equal`, `unequal`, `prop("Name")` |
| Text | `length`, `substring`, `contains`, `test`, `match`, `replace` (the first match), `replaceAll`, `lower`, `upper`, `trim`, `repeat`, `split`, `join`, `format`, `concat` |
| Numbers | `add`, `subtract`, `multiply`, `divide`, `mod`, `pow`, `abs`, `round(n, places)`, `ceil`, `floor`, `sqrt`, `cbrt`, `sign`, `exp`, `ln`, `log10`, `log2`, `sum`, `mean`, `median`, `toNumber`, `pi`, `e` |
| Dates | `dateAdd`, `dateSubtract`, `dateBetween`, `formatDate`, `parseDate`, `timestamp`, `fromTimestamp`, `year`, `month` (1–12), `week` (ISO), `day` (1 = Monday … 7 = Sunday), `dayOfMonth` (Notion's `date()`), `hour`, `minute` |
| Lists | `map`, `filter`, `find`, `findIndex`, `some`, `every`, `count`: the expression sees `current` and `index`. `at` (a negative index counts from the end), `first`, `last`, `slice`, `sort`, `reverse`, `unique`, `includes`, `flat` |
| Relations | `relation.<name>` (the related notes), `current.prop("X")` on one of them, `lookup(relation.<name>, "X")`, `rollup.<name>` |
| Hebrew | `hebrewDate(date)` gives "ב׳ בכסלו תשפ״ז", and `hebrewDate(date, "day" \| "month" \| "year")` one part. `stripNikud(text)` removes the vowel marks |

`dateBetween(a, b, unit)` is a − b in whole units, toward zero, as in
Notion. Units are years, quarters, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes,
seconds and milliseconds. An empty date or number gives an empty result, so
a row without the property shows nothing instead of an error.

## Examples

```yaml
relations:
  subs: { property: Parent, incoming: true }
formulas:
  daysLeft: dateBetween(Due, today(), "days")
  hours: sum(map(relation.subs, current.prop("Estimate")))
  done: round(count(relation.subs, current.prop("Done")) / length(relation.subs) * 100) + "%"
  priority: ifs(Priority == 1, "High", Priority == 2, "Medium", "Low")
  hebrew: hebrewDate(Due)
```

## For scripts and plugins

A plugin with the `bases:read` permission reads a view's rows with
`lumen.bases.query()`. With `bases:write`, `lumen.bases.update()` changes note
properties behind one approval screen per call. See
[Plugin API](/plugins/api/). Automations can run
[when a row of a base changes](/workspace/automations/).

## Speed

10,000 notes, with two filters for every view, one view filter, a formula
column and a two-key sort, run in tens of milliseconds once warm. Simple
filter statements (a property compared with a value, `file.inFolder`,
`file.hasTag`, and `&&`, `||`, `!` of those) run without the interpreter,
with the same results.

## How it was checked

A golden set of 53 formulas as Notion users write them, with the values
Notion documents (`src/__tests__/basesNotion.test.ts`), uses every function
above.
